opening.headline: When release criteria vary by business unit and risks are not uniform, we learn how to combine evaluation, safety, and operational criteria into a single release gate.
body: Even among services using the same model, the pre-launch review standards can vary by business unit. Some business units release products based solely on evaluation results, others conduct only security reviews, while others release without any specific criteria. When incidents occur in units with lower standards, trust in the entire organization is undermined.

In this course, we examine release gates from three perspectives: safety, security, and operations. Using a model where vendors verify safety measures prior to release, we review an example release checklist and then follow a case study that illustrates issues arising from different departments with varying criteria, as well as the process of introducing common gates.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Evaluations, safety, and operational criteria can be aggregated into a single release gate for analysis.
It can be determined whether the launch criteria are consistent across business units.

screens.title: Launch criteria vary by business unit, leading to uneven risks.
screens.lead:
First, read about the scenario where three business units launch services using the same model but apply different criteria.

As of 2026-10, RSP v3.4 represents a policy that jointly considers risk mitigation measures, Frontier Safety Roadmap, and Risk Reports. It does not solely rely on past ASL stage descriptions to define current training and deployment conditions.

visual.alt: The three business units are launching over different height thresholds.
labels: Business Division B: Security review only
The weakest point is determining trust between entities.

paragraphs: Let's assume each of the three business units develops and launches its own service using the same model. Business Unit A reviews only the evaluation results, Business Unit B conducts only a security review, and Business Unit C launches without any additional criteria.

The model is the same, but the inspection standards at launch differ. When an incident occurs in a business unit with lower standards, it does not remain solely a unit-level issue—it undermines the company's overall trust. When risks are not uniform, the weakest point determines the entire organization's reputation.

Service providers also include a step to verify whether safety mechanisms are sufficient prior to launch. OpenAI requires that high-capability systems have safety mechanisms in place before deployment, and the evaluation best practices document identifies delaying evaluation after launch as an anti-pattern. The question for this lesson is this: how can we integrate evaluation, safety, and operational criteria into a single launch gate?

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The release gate is a approval checkpoint at which all predefined criteria must be satisfied before proceeding to the next stage.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what conditions are required for launch approval.

screens.title: Are there any conditions required for launch approval?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Are there any conditions required for launch approval? Are these conditions documented, or are they based on the practices of the responsible personnel?
items.answer: Practices-based conditions vanish when the responsible party changes and are interpreted differently across business units. Conditions must be formally documented so that anyone can assess them using the same standard.

items.prompt: Based on the evaluation results, safety review, and operational readiness, what areas are being overlooked?
items.answer: If a domain is missing, an incident will also occur within that domain. If evaluation is missing, quality degradation will go unnoticed; if safety is missing, the system will fail to respond to misuse; if operations are missing, there will be no way to revert during outages.

items.prompt: Does a release actually halt if the conditions are not met?
items.answer: Even if there are criteria, if they are not satisfied, then the release will not stop—those criteria become mere decoration. Unlike a checklist, a gate prevents progression to the next stage if it is not passed.

screens.outro: Now let's examine the three axes that constitute the launch gate.

screens.title: The three axes of launch gates: evaluation, safety, operations
screens.lead: Select each tab to confirm the three axes that form the release gate and their respective references.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the launch gate placed on the three pillars of evaluation, safety, and operations.
labels: If one axis is missing, the gate will not open.

tabs.label: Evaluation criteria
tabs.body: This is a continuous evaluation system where goals, metrics, and benchmarks are established, and evaluations are repeatedly conducted whenever changes occur. The OpenAI evaluation document explains that evaluations should be performed frequently and early, using data that reflects operational traffic, and should not be postponed until after launch.

tabs.label: Safety standards
tabs.body: This is a condition to verify that appropriate safety mechanisms are in place and that human review pathways are established according to risk classification. Vendors are also required to conduct a review during pre-launch to ensure that safety mechanisms are sufficient. OpenAI's operational documentation advises referring separately to safety best practices.

tabs.label: Operational Standards
tabs.body: Operational prerequisites such as API key management, spending limits, and monitoring. OpenAI's operational documentation recommends against hardcoding keys in code, instead suggesting exposure through environment variables or secret management services, and advises setting expiration periods and regular rotation procedures. It also recommends configuring spending alerts and hard spending limits, as well as separating staging and production projects.

tabs.label: read together
tabs.body: Google's Well-Architected perspectives advise considering operational excellence, security, reliability, cost, and performance together. The launch gate requires passing all three axes; if one axis is lacking, the gate will not open regardless of how strong the others are.

screens.outro: By observing how vendors make their release decisions, gate design can be informed.

screens.title: The vendor framework's release decision structure
screens.lead: While reading the table, compare how the three providers bundle evaluation and safety review into a single decision point.

data.caption: Release decision structure by provider
rows: Capability Report and Safety Device Report
The Safety Advisory Group reviewed both reports, assessed the remaining risks, and provided recommendations to the executive management.
A system with high capability is deployed after safety mechanisms have sufficiently reduced the risk.
Current RSP risk assessment, mitigation actions, and report
Verify policy version and evaluation rationale in the report
Distinguish current actions from objectives and do not arbitrarily determine based on past ASL bulk conditions

data.notes: The fact that the three companies' procedures share the same single gate does not mean that they are identical. Organizations should refer to each provider's evaluation and controls, but must clearly specify their own launch approvers and evaluation, safety, and operational criteria.

screens.outro: Now, let's read an example of a release checklist that includes this structure.

screens.title: Launch checklist example
screens.lead: The following is a hypothetical release checklist grouped by three axes. Selecting the indicated sections allows you to see which axis each item belongs to and why it is necessary.

data.text:
[Evaluation] Compared to the benchmark, the result is Meets the predefined threshold value. The distribution of operational inputs is reflected in the evaluation bundle.  
[Safety] There are safety devices and personnel review paths corresponding to the risk classification..  
[Operation] Monitoring metrics, thresholds, alerting paths, and rollback paths are defined..  
[Operation] Keys should be stored in environment variables or a secret management service and Expiration and replacement procedures exist.. Expense limit notification is set.  
[Responsibility] Release approval authorities and exception approval procedures are specified..

marks.note: This is at the core of the evaluation axis. The baseline must be established before viewing the results, as this is what enables the gate to actually filter outcomes. The distribution of operational inputs must be reflected in the evaluation batch, which is also why OpenAI's evaluation documentation cautions against biased design.

marks.span: There are safety devices and personnel review paths corresponding to the risk classification.
marks.note: This is a safety consideration. It verifies that appropriate safety measures are in place for the types of risks handled by the service, and that there is a human review pathway for cases that cannot be automatically filtered.

marks.span: Monitoring metrics, thresholds, alerting paths, and rollback paths are defined.
marks.note: This is an operational requirement. After release, there must be means to detect quality degradation or errors, and a path to roll back when issues occur. If either of these is missing, the system cannot detect or respond to failures.

This is key management as recommended in OpenAI's operational documentation. Set expiration dates on keys and establish a regular rotation procedure, and before rotating keys, update the application to use the new key, then verify that the previous key no longer functions before retiring it.

This is an expenditure alert that notifies when usage exceeds a certain amount. The document explains that when the hard expenditure limit is reached, the corresponding API traffic will be halted; therefore, the impact must be reviewed before enabling it in an operational environment.

marks.span: Release approval authorities and exception approval procedures are specified.
marks.note: This is a responsibility item. To prevent unauthorized bypassing of the gate, it must be clearly defined who is authorized to open the gate and the procedures to be followed when an item is exempted.

screens.outro: Let's follow an example to see what happens when the standards differ.

screens.title: Explanation: Issues caused by inconsistencies in standards among business units
screens.lead: Select an item to expand and verify how the different criteria across the three business divisions lead to distinct considerations.

items.title: Assumption example
items.body: The three business units launched services using the same model, but they have different launch criteria. While the model is identical, the areas inspected prior to launch vary by business unit.

items.title: Division A: Operational readiness is not established.
items.body: Division A conducted the assessment but did not carry out operational readiness. Since the assessment results were positive, it appeared there would be no issues with launch. However, because there was no rollback path in case of failure, once a problem was detected, the service could not be restored to its original state.

items.title: Business Division B: Evaluation is absent.
items.body: Division B had conducted only security reviews and no assessments. Even if product quality gradually deteriorated after launch, without a baseline benchmark, such degradation would go undetected until users raised complaints.

items.title: Division C: No loan limit notification received
items.body: Division C did not receive expenditure limit notifications. Even if responses become longer or calls increase, the absence of notifications causes costs to rise unexpectedly. The OpenAI operations document states that expenditure notifications and hard expenditure limits can be set.

items.title: Results from a corporate perspective
items.body: These three incidents may appear different, but they all stem from the same root cause: the absence of a common gate. Even when using the same model, the pre-launch inspection scope varies by business unit, resulting in different manifestations of the incidents depending on which areas were overlooked. When risks are uneven, it is the weakest business unit that determines the company's overall reputation.

screens.outro: Then, how should we introduce the common gate? We will address this next.

screens.title: Explanation: Introduction of common release gate and exception handling
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the procedure for introducing a common gate step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Defines the minimum items collectively for the corporation.
steps.body: Define the minimum items under the three pillars of evaluation, safety, and operations as a corporate common gate. If the list becomes too lengthy, field teams will be unable to comply, so it includes only those items that are absolutely necessary for all services.

steps.title: Reduced according to risk
steps.body: For high-risk services, add items, and for low-risk services, provide a simplified path. This way, the common gateway maintains consistency while operating in a realistic manner.

steps.title: Log the exception and reevaluate.
steps.body: Exceptions record the approver, reason, and expiration date. Exceptions without such records cannot be explained later for why they were waived, and may easily become entrenched as practice. Exceptions that have expired are subject to periodic review to determine whether they should be maintained or revoked.

steps.title: Aggregates results to refresh the benchmark
steps.body: Aggregate gate outcomes and incident records to update baselines. If the same item repeatedly leads to issues, strengthen that item; if an item is unrelated to any incidents, review it for simplification. These updates are necessary to prevent the gate from diverging from reality.

steps.title: result
steps.body: The common gate ensures consistency, while risk-based items provide practicality. The previous structure, in which the weakest business unit determined overall trust when no common gate existed, is now replaced. However, introducing a common gate is not the end; ongoing observation of exceptions and incidents is required to continuously refine and improve the process.

screens.outro: Finally, let's summarize the configuration based on the release criteria.

screens.title: The release criteria are the combination of evaluation, safety, and operation.
screens.lead: This summarizes the launch criteria covered in this class.

paragraphs: **Evaluation Criteria** consists of indicators and benchmark values, with continuous evaluation. Benchmark values are established before viewing the results, and the evaluation is performed again each time changes are made.

**Safety Requirements** are safety devices and review processes aligned with risk classification. The approach where service providers combine evaluations and safety reviews into a single decision point serves as a model.

**Operational criteria** include monitoring, threshold alerts, rollback, and key management. All three axes must be passed for the gate to open; the common gate ensures consistency, while risk-specific criteria ensure realism. With this structure, even if business units differ, they will answer the same questions before release, and we can confidently state that any service from any business unit has undergone at least a minimal level of review.

callout.label: Core
callout.text: If even one axle is missing, the gate will not open.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: A service has passed the evaluation criteria and security review, but lacks monitoring metrics, alerting pathways, and rollback procedures. How would a common release gate assess this scenario?
options: Since both axes have been passed through, operational readiness will be addressed post-launch and the launch will proceed.
Since the operational axis is insufficient, the gate remains closed; it is then reassessed after compensation is applied.
If the evaluation result is very good, the operation axis is exempted and the gate is opened.
A safety review can be conducted again to replace the operational axis.
checks.explain: The gate must pass through all three axes of evaluation, safety, and operation. If any one axis is insufficient, the gate will not open even if the others are satisfactory.

wrong.0: Without operational readiness, there are no methods to roll back during failures and no means to detect them.
wrong.2: Exception approval is required to follow an exception procedure recording the approver, reason, and deadline, and automatic exemption does not occur based on evaluation results.
wrong.3: Safety review and operational readiness are distinct domains and cannot be substituted for one another.

checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The gate opens only when all three axes pass through.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. When one axis is missing, check whether another axis can take its place.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.
checks.q: Review the procedure for introducing a common release gate in the correct order.
items: Defines the minimum items under the three pillars of evaluation, safety, and operation as a corporate common gate.
For high-risk services, add items; for low-risk services, provide a simplified path.
Exceptions are recorded with approver, reason, and deadline and are regularly reviewed.
Aggregates gate results and incident records to update the baseline.
checks.explain: The flow involves first establishing a common baseline, then applying adjustments based on risk levels, managing exceptions, and aggregating results to update the standards.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. It begins with a common base and proceeds through updates.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Review the order again. Risk-based deductions are only possible with a common foundation.

glossary.def: Approval checkpoint requires passing all predefined criteria before proceeding to the next stage.
This is a quality condition involving setting objectives, indicators, and benchmark values, and verifying them each time there is a change.
This is a condition to verify that appropriate safety devices and review pathways are in place according to the risk classification.
This is a condition for viewing operational readiness, such as monitoring, threshold alerts, rollbacks, and key management.
This is a procedure for recording the approver, reason, and deadline when exempting a gate item.

misconceptions.myth: Approval alone is sufficient for release.
misconceptions.fact: Without safety and operational criteria, accidents and cost issues remain. The release criteria consist of evaluation, safety, and operational factors.

misconceptions.myth: When business units are given autonomy, site-specific standards are established.
misconceptions.fact: Since risks are not uniform, the weakest business unit ends up determining the company's overall trust. This approach of adding risk-based items at a common gate also provides realism.

misconceptions.myth: A gate, once set, is fixed.
misconceptions.fact: Gate outcomes and incident records should be aggregated to continuously update the baseline.

closing.lead: This summarizes the core content of the class.
points: The release criteria are the sum of evaluation, safety, and operation.
If even one axle is missing, the gate will not open.

The common gate ensures consistency, while risk-based items ensure practicality. With this structure, even if business units differ, they will answer the same questions before launch, and we can reasonably state that any service from any business unit has undergone at least a basic review.
